title: Prices in Python
summary: Use integers, division, and formatted strings to print exact prices.

scenario.briefing: A Python report prints 12.5 instead of 12.50. Repair format_price so cents render with two decimal places and a dollar sign.

objectives.description: Render integer cents as an exact price string.
Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Integer division // gives whole dollars. Remainder % gives cents.
Cents need two digits, including a leading zero.
Use an f-string with :02d on the remainder.

misconceptions.description: Using true division and losing the two-digit cents format.
misconceptions.testDescription: A normal price uses two decimals.
misconceptions.feedback: True division produces a float. Work with integer dollars and integer cents so formatting stays exact.

misconceptions.description: Formatting cents without a leading zero for values under ten.
misconceptions.testDescription: Five cents keeps the leading zero.
misconceptions.feedback: Five cents must render as 05 in the cents position. The :02d format specifier supplies the leading zero.

misconceptions.description: Assuming every decimal price is exactly representable as a float.
misconceptions.feedback: Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point. Format integer cents instead.

sections.title: Python values have types
sections.body: An int is a whole number, a float has a fractional part, and a str is text. Integer division with // discards the remainder, while % returns it. Formatting a number is a presentation decision, not a new value.

sections.title: Format widths preserve meaning
sections.body: The format specifier 02d means at least two digits, padded with a leading zero. Without it, five cents becomes .5 instead of .05. Exact formatting matters for money and identifiers.
